# Wirecard Public-Fraud Trail: Company Statements, Audit Uncertainty, Missing Cash, Supervisory Failure, and Jan Marsalek

## Scope and evidentiary method

This report reconstructs the Wirecard public-fraud trail using only the two supplied sources. The first source is Wirecard AG’s regulatory announcement of 28 April 2020 concerning delivery of the KPMG special-investigation report. The second is a European Parliament Economic Governance Support Unit study examining the supervisory implications of the Wirecard scandal. The sources are identified below as **S1** and **S2** for the structured evidence object at the end of this report.

The evidence supports a clear conclusion about the public information trail: Wirecard’s own communications presented the KPMG investigation as having found no incriminating evidence of balance-sheet forgery, while the later-described contents of the KPMG report were substantially more qualified. KPMG reportedly could not verify the existence and accuracy of significant third-party-acquiring revenues and was unable to locate or verify approximately €1 billion in trust-account balances. The subsequent discovery that €1.9 billion in reported bank balances probably did not exist, followed by insolvency proceedings, transformed an apparently reassuring corporate narrative into evidence of a severe financial-reporting failure.

The supplied sources do **not**, however, provide evidence sufficient to establish Jan Marsalek’s whereabouts, the circumstances of his disappearance, or a proven relationship between his disappearance and the accounting fraud. Those matters must therefore remain outside the factual conclusions of this report.

## Executive findings

### Principal conclusion

The strongest evidence-based assessment is that Wirecard’s 28 April 2020 announcement was materially more reassuring than the underlying KPMG findings described in the European Parliament study. Wirecard stated that no incriminating evidence of balance-sheet forgery had been identified and that available audit documents were sufficient to prove third-party-acquiring revenues for 2016–2018. The parliamentary study, drawing on the KPMG report, states that KPMG could neither confirm nor refute whether relevant third-party-acquiring revenues existed or were correctly stated and could not verify approximately €1 billion in trust accounts. ([Wirecard AG, 2020](https://www.wirecard.com/2020/04/22/wirecard-ag-kpmg-special-review-lasts-until-april-27-2020-analysis-so-far-provides-no-evidence-of-balance-sheet-manipulation); [Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

This discrepancy does not, by itself, prove that the 28 April announcement was deliberately fraudulent. It does support the assessment that the announcement communicated a conclusion of reassurance while the forensic investigation remained unable to verify core financial assertions.

### Public-fraud trail in brief

| Date | Public development | Evidentiary significance |
|---|---|---|
| 2008 | Shareholder association SdK allegedly questioned Wirecard’s margins and treatment of customer deposits. | Early warning described in the parliamentary study. |
| 2015 onward | Financial Times reporting raised alleged accounting inconsistencies. | Persistent external allegations and information flow. |
| 2016 | Zatarra Report accused Wirecard of corruption, fraud, and money laundering. | Allegation, not a finding established by the supplied sources. |
| January–February 2019 | Financial Times reported alleged forged or backdated contracts; BaFin referred accounts to FREP. | Formal supervisory response began under Germany’s two-step system. |
| February 2019 | BaFin prohibited establishing or increasing net short positions in Wirecard shares. | Intervention potentially restricted a market-based source of negative information. |
| October 2019 | Wirecard hired KPMG for a special forensic investigation. | Company-commissioned investigation into public allegations. |
| April 2020 | Wirecard said no incriminating evidence had been found; KPMG reportedly could not verify approximately €1 billion in trust accounts. | Central contradiction in the public record. |
| June 2020 | Wirecard acknowledged that €1.9 billion in trust-account balances probably did not exist. | Escalation from uncertainty to probable non-existence of reported cash. |
| June 2020 | Wirecard filed for insolvency. | Collapse of the company’s financial and governance framework. |

The chronology is based on the timeline and source descriptions in the parliamentary study. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

## Reconstruction of the public-fraud trail

### Early warnings and recurring allegations

The parliamentary study describes warnings dating back to at least 2008. The shareholder association SdK allegedly accused Wirecard of reporting unusually high margins and treating customer deposits as its own cash. In 2015, Financial Times reporting began raising questions about accounting inconsistencies, particularly concerning Wirecard’s Singapore operations. In 2016, the Zatarra Report accused Wirecard of corruption, fraud, and money laundering. These were allegations and warnings, not judicial findings established by the supplied evidence. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

The parliamentary study emphasizes that the warning signals came from several channels: employees, journalists, analysts, short sellers, and external critics. It also notes that the relevant information was not consistently taken seriously by management, auditors, or supervisors. The study expressly cautions against hindsight bias, acknowledging that early warnings can be mixed with inaccurate complaints or market-manipulation attempts. Nevertheless, its assessment is that several potentially important information sources were “silenced, or at least not sufficiently heard.” ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

This is important because the Wirecard case was not presented in the supplied evidence as a fraud that emerged without warning. Rather, it appears as a prolonged accumulation of unresolved allegations, partial investigations, and institutional responses that failed to produce a timely and authoritative resolution.

### 2019: supervisory intervention and the short-selling ban

On 30 January 2019, the Financial Times reported that Wirecard allegedly used forged and backdated contracts to increase revenues. On 15 February, BaFin directed the Financial Reporting Enforcement Panel, known as FREP, to examine Wirecard’s interim group accounts as of 30 June 2018. On 18 February, BaFin prohibited the establishment of new net short positions and increases in existing net short positions in Wirecard shares until 18 April 2019. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

The parliamentary study’s assessment is critical of this intervention. It argues that short selling can help incorporate negative information into market prices and that a short-selling prohibition is asymmetric because it restricts downward pressure without imposing a corresponding restriction on optimistic positions. The authors conclude that the ban may have harmed investors who subsequently bought shares at excessive prices. They recommend that short-selling prohibitions be restricted to circumstances involving market-wide or systemic risk. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

The evidence does not establish that the ban caused the later collapse. It does support a narrower conclusion: according to the parliamentary study, the intervention may have impaired one mechanism through which skeptical information could have been reflected in Wirecard’s share price and acted upon by investors, banks, rating agencies, and supervisors.

### The two-step enforcement structure

The supplied study identifies Germany’s two-step financial-reporting enforcement structure as a central institutional weakness. Under that structure, FREP generally conducted the first examination while BaFin retained enforcement authority in specified circumstances. FREP was a private body with a public mandate and lacked statutory investigative powers, meaning that it relied substantially on the cooperation of the company under examination. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

The study reports that FREP conducted random checks of Wirecard’s 2011 and 2014 accounts without discovering reporting errors. Following the 2019 Financial Times reports, BaFin requested that FREP examine Wirecard’s interim accounts. The authors argue that the structure created latency, unclear responsibility, and a “wait-and-see” dynamic in which the public supervisor was not the immediate primary investigator. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

The study’s conclusion is not that the legal framework made investigation impossible. It notes that there was debate over whether BaFin could have taken over an investigation on the basis of “improper execution of control” by FREP. Rather, the problem was that responsibilities and powers were sufficiently fragmented to delay decisive public intervention. The authors therefore recommend making BaFin the sole competent authority, with bodies such as FREP serving only in a delegated or ancillary capacity. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

## The KPMG investigation and the company’s public statements

### Wirecard’s 28 April announcement

Wirecard’s 28 April 2020 regulatory announcement stated that KPMG had delivered its special-investigation report. The announcement said that “incriminating evidence” for public allegations of balance-sheet forgery had not been identified. It further stated that, across the four audit areas—third-party acquiring, merchant cash advance/digital lending, and business activities in India and Singapore—no significant findings required adjustment of the 2016–2018 annual accounts. ([Wirecard AG, 2020](https://www.wirecard.com/2020/04/22/wirecard-ag-kpmg-special-review-lasts-until-april-27-2020-analysis-so-far-provides-no-evidence-of-balance-sheet-manipulation))

Wirecard also stated that the documents and audit measures available during the ordinary audits had been sufficient to prove third-party-acquiring revenues. It acknowledged that KPMG had not obtained all data required under heightened forensic standards because relevant data were primarily controlled by third parties. Wirecard then emphasized that more than 200 million data sets relating to December 2019 had been supplied to KPMG and that the forensic audit had identified no deviations between reported revenues and account balances. ([Wirecard AG, 2020](https://www.wirecard.com/2020/04/22/wirecard-ag-kpmg-special-review-lasts-until-april-27-2020-analysis-so-far-provides-no-evidence-of-balance-sheet-manipulation))

The announcement therefore used several layers of qualification but led with a strongly exculpatory message: no incriminating evidence, no material findings requiring restatement, and no deviations in the December 2019 data tested.

### The KPMG uncertainty described by the parliamentary study

The parliamentary study presents a materially less conclusive account. It states that KPMG was unable to locate or verify approximately €1 billion in foreign trust accounts because of insufficient documentation from Wirecard and its third-party acquirers. It further states that KPMG could neither refute nor confirm the allegations. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

The study quotes the KPMG position that, concerning revenues from relevant third-party-acquiring relationships, KPMG could not make a statement that the revenues existed and were correct in amount, nor could it make a statement that they did not exist or were incorrect. This is a forensic non-verification, not an exoneration. The distinction is fundamental: failure to prove fraud is not proof that the underlying revenues and bank balances were genuine. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

### Assessment of the contradiction

The apparent contradiction can be stated precisely:

1. **Wirecard’s framing:** no incriminating evidence of balance-sheet forgery had been identified; ordinary audit evidence was sufficient to prove revenues; and the tested December 2019 data showed no deviations. ([Wirecard AG, 2020](https://www.wirecard.com/2020/04/22/wirecard-ag-kpmg-special-review-lasts-until-april-27-2020-analysis-so-far-provides-no-evidence-of-balance-sheet-manipulation))
2. **KPMG findings as summarized by the parliamentary study:** KPMG could not verify approximately €1 billion in trust accounts and could neither confirm nor refute whether important third-party-acquiring revenues existed and were correctly stated. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))
3. **Later company position:** by 22 June 2020, Wirecard’s board assumed that €1.9 billion in trust-account balances probably did not exist and that the third-party business might be incorrect as previously described. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

My assessment is that the 28 April statement should be treated as an example of corporate communication that emphasized the absence of a definitive forensic finding while minimizing the significance of unresolved verification failures. The supplied evidence does not prove the announcement was knowingly false at the moment it was issued. It does show that the announcement did not provide investors with the full practical significance of KPMG’s inability to verify critical assets and revenue streams.

## Missing cash and collapse

The reported cash problem escalated rapidly. The parliamentary study states that KPMG could not verify roughly €1 billion in trust accounts in April 2020. On 22 June, Wirecard’s board stated that the €1.9 billion in trust accounts probably did not exist. On 25 June, Wirecard filed for insolvency because of impending insolvency and over-indebtedness. The study also states that EY refused to sign off the 2019 accounts after identifying forged bank confirmations and “clear indications” of a sophisticated fraud involving multiple parties and institutions. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

The progression from “not all data could be obtained” to “approximately €1 billion could not be verified,” then to “€1.9 billion probably did not exist,” is the central financial arc of the public-fraud trail. It demonstrates that the issue was not merely an accounting classification dispute. The evidence describes a substantial gap between reported cash balances and balances that could be independently verified.

The supplied evidence also identifies weaknesses in the external-audit environment. EY had issued unqualified opinions on Wirecard’s financial statements for earlier years, while the KPMG investigation questioned whether the trust accounts were properly classified as cash or cash equivalents under IFRS. The study further reports allegations that EY relied on confirmations issued in the name of a trustee rather than independently verifying the relevant bank accounts. These points are presented in the study as matters requiring scrutiny, not as a final adjudication of EY’s legal liability. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

## Supervisory and governance failures

The parliamentary study concludes that all five lines of defense failed in some manner: internal controls, the supervisory board, external audit, oversight bodies for financial reporting and auditing, and BaFin. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

Its specific criticisms include:

- inadequate internal controls and documentation;
- insufficiently independent supervisory-board oversight;
- failure of external audit processes to detect or adequately respond to warning signals;
- weaknesses in audit oversight and limited public transparency concerning audit-firm inspections;
- a fragmented financial-reporting enforcement system;
- insufficient or delayed supervisory action by BaFin;
- failure to treat whistleblowers, investigative journalism, and short selling as potentially valuable information sources.

The authors recommend legally requiring effective internal-control systems for listed firms, strengthening audit committees, requiring the head of internal control or compliance to report to the supervisory board, increasing auditor liability, improving audit-oversight transparency, and granting supervisors stronger investigative powers. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

They also propose a European Single Capital Market Supervisor, or ESCMS, because fraud involving a major European issuer can create cross-border spillovers and because national supervisors may be affected by domestic political or economic interests. This is a policy proposal, not an institution shown by the sources to have been created or operationalized. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

## Jan Marsalek and the limits of the supplied evidence

The target query asks for the public-fraud trail and Jan Marsalek’s disappearance. The supplied materials do not mention Jan Marsalek by name. They do not provide:

- a date or location of his disappearance;
- evidence concerning his travel, identity documents, or alleged aliases;
- evidence of his role in the missing cash;
- evidence that he was responsible for falsified bank confirmations;
- evidence linking his disappearance to Wirecard’s insolvency;
- evidence concerning any criminal charge, arrest warrant, intelligence relationship, or current whereabouts.

Accordingly, no factual conclusion about Marsalek’s disappearance can be responsibly drawn from these sources. Any narrative linking him to the missing €1.9 billion or treating his disappearance as proof of involvement would exceed the evidence supplied. The appropriate conclusion is therefore **evidentiary absence**, not exoneration or implication.

## Overall assessment

The supplied evidence supports the following concrete opinion:

> Wirecard’s public communications in April 2020 projected confidence at precisely the point when the underlying forensic investigation remained unable to verify essential revenue and cash claims. The company’s subsequent acknowledgment that €1.9 billion probably did not exist, combined with the parliamentary study’s account of fragmented supervision and failed audit defenses, indicates a systemic public-fraud trail characterized by repeated warnings, delayed escalation, insufficient verification, and over-reassuring disclosure. The materials do not establish Jan Marsalek’s role in, or connection to, the disappearance.

The case is therefore best understood not as a single missed audit error, but as a multi-layer failure of information processing. External warnings existed; short sellers and journalists raised concerns; supervisors initiated examinations; auditors issued clean opinions; and the company commissioned a special investigation. Yet the system did not convert the warning signals into timely, authoritative verification of the company’s most important assets and revenue streams.

## References

Langenbucher, K., Leuz, C., Kra hnen, J. P., & Pelizzon, L. (2020). *What are the wider supervisory implications of the Wirecard case?* Economic Governance Support Unit, Directorate-General for Internal Policies, European Parliament.
